sections.title: 1. OS Fundamentals, SO3 & Memory Addressing (C1 & E1)
sections.description: What an OS kernel does, multitasking vs monotasking, the SO3 environment, byte-addressable memory, SI vs IEC units, and little-endian pointer manipulation in C.

blocks.title: What Is an Operating System Kernel?
blocks.content:
An **Operating System (OS)** is the central software layer that mediates between physical hardware and user applications. In this course, we focus on the **kernel**—the privileged core of the OS.

### Two Perspectives
- **User perspective:** Provides a clean execution environment (abstractions) and enforces protection between programs.
- **System perspective:** Manages physical & logical resources (CPU, RAM, I/O devices, files) and enforces isolation.

### Core Kernel Subsystems (E2 Q3)
1. **Process & Thread Management / Scheduler** — Decides which task runs on which CPU core and when.
2. **Memory Manager** — Allocates RAM, isolates address spaces, and configures the MMU.
3. **Filesystem (VFS)** — Abstracts storage devices into files, directories, and descriptors.
4. **Inter-Process Communication (IPC) & Network Stack** — Enables safe communication (pipes, signals, sockets).
5. **Device Drivers & HAL** — Hardware Abstraction Layer interfacing with controllers.

### Monotasking vs. Multitasking (E2 Q1)
- **Monotasking:** Only one application resides in RAM at a time. Switching requires slow **swapping** (swap-out / swap-in) to secondary storage.
- **Multitasking:** Multiple applications reside in RAM simultaneously. CPU switches rapidly between them (**time-sharing**), dramatically increasing CPU utilization. Requires a memory manager (to place programs, often using **relocatable code**) and a **scheduler**.

blocks.title: The SO3 Teaching OS & Lab Environment
blocks.content:
**SO3 (Smart Object Oriented OS)** is a lightweight, open-source OS developed at REDS/HEIG-VD (GPLv2), written in **C and ARM assembly** using Linux's **KBuild** system.

- **Target Hardware:** 32-bit ARM Cortex-A15 (emulated via **QEMU `virt32` / vExpress** inside a Linux host VM).
- **Why SO3?** Small enough to read and modify end-to-end while faithfully modeling modern Unix/Linux kernel subsystems (VFS, pipes, scheduler, MMU, syscalls).
- **Debugging:** VS Code + `gdb` attached over TCP/IP (`localhost:1234`) to QEMU.

blocks.title: Byte-Addressable Memory, Bit Widths & SI vs. IEC Units (C1 & E1)
blocks.content:
A **byte-adressable** system assigns a unique address to every single **byte (8 bits)**—the smallest addressable unit of memory. (Individual bits inside a byte are accessed via bitwise arithmetic/logic instructions, not separate addresses.)

### Address Space Size Formula
If CPU address registers are $n$ bits wide, the processor can reference $2^n$ distinct bytes, from `0x0` to $2^n - 1$:

$$\text{Addressable Bytes} = 2^n \quad\Longrightarrow\quad n = \log_2(\text{Bytes})$$

- **32-bit CPU:** $2^{32}\text{ bytes} = 4\text{ GiB}$, spanning `0x0000'0000` to `0xffff'ffff`.
- **Region Size Formula (E1 Q1):** For an inclusive range $[A_{\text{start}}, A_{\text{end}}]$:

$$\text{Size} = A_{\text{end}} - A_{\text{start}} + 1$$

> [!WARNING]
> **Classic Off-by-One Trap (E1 Q1 & Q3):**
> - Range `0x1000` to `0xf'ffff`: Size $= \text{0x100000} - \text{0x1000} = \text{0xff000} = 1044480\text{ bytes}$ ($1020\text{ KiB}$), **not** `0xf'efff`!
> - An $8\text{ KiB}$ ($8192 = 2^{13} = \text{0x2000}$) region starting at `0x0` ends at `0x2000 - 1 = 0x1fff`.

### Binary (IEC) vs. Decimal (SI) Units (E1 Q4)
| Context | Prefix | Exact Value |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **RAM / Address Space** | $1\text{ KiB}, 1\text{ MiB}, 1\text{ GiB}$ | $2^{10} = 1024,\; 2^{20},\; 2^{30}$ bytes |
| **Storage (HDD/SSD marketing)** | $500\text{ GB}$ (SI) | $500 \times 10^9$ bytes ($\approx 465.66\text{ GiB}$) |

A "500 GB" hard drive has $500 \times 10^9$ bytes, which an OS reporting in binary GiB displays as $\approx 465.7\text{ GiB}$ (plus reserved/bad-block sectors).

blocks.title: Address Bus Width to Addressable Memory
blocks.description: Adjust the address width in bits (n) to compute total addressable memory in MiB (2^n / 2^20). For example, 256 MiB = 2^8 * 2^20 = 2^28 bytes -> 28 bits (E1 Q2).

sections.title: 2. Hardware Architecture, CPU Modes & Interrupts (C2 & E2)
sections.description: Synchronous vs asynchronous hardware requests, MMU address translation, User vs Kernel mode, hardware IRQs vs software traps, SMP multicore, and Monolithic vs Microkernel architectures.

blocks.title: CPU–Hardware Interaction & the MMU
blocks.content:
From the OS perspective, hardware interaction consists of two request directions:
1. **CPU $\rightarrow$ Outside (Synchronous):** Reading/writing RAM, sending commands to device controllers over the bus (PCI, AHB). Initiated by the CPU and executed immediately.
2. **Outside $\rightarrow$ CPU (Asynchronous):** **Hardware Interrupts (IRQs)**. A device controller asserts a dedicated electrical line through an Interrupt Controller (e.g., **APIC**) to notify the CPU (e.g., disk read finished, timer tick).

### The Memory Management Unit (MMU)
Modern CPUs do not send raw physical RAM addresses directly when an MMU is active. Instead:
- The CPU emits **Virtual Addresses** (even during instruction fetch).
- The **MMU** translates each virtual address into a **Physical Address** in RAM and enforces memory protection (preventing user apps from touching kernel memory or I/O registers).

blocks.title: User Mode vs. Kernel Mode & Interrupt Types (C2 & E2)
blocks.content:
To protect the OS and other applications, the CPU enforces two primary execution modes:

| Feature | User Mode | Kernel (Supervisor) Mode (E2 Q5) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Who runs here?** | User applications | OS Kernel, ISRs, (and drivers in monolithic OS) |
| **Privileged instructions** | **Forbidden** (triggers trap) | **Allowed** (I/O access, status register, MMU, coprocessors) |
| **Memory access** | Restricted to own virtual space | Full access to kernel & I/O regions |

### Mode Transitions (Critical Exam Topic!)
- **At boot:** CPU starts in **Kernel Mode**.
- **Kernel $\rightarrow$ User:** Kernel modifies the CPU status register (a privileged instruction) and jumps to user code.
- **User $\rightarrow$ Kernel:** **Impossible** directly! Can **only** happen via an interrupt:
  - **Hardware Interrupt (IRQ — Asynchronous):** Timer tick, keyboard, disk DMA completion. Ensures no infinite loop in user space can monopolize the CPU (E2 Q4: the **hardware timer IRQ** preempts it!).
  - **Software Interrupt / Exception / Trap (Synchronous):** Triggered by executing an instruction—either an error (divide by zero, invalid memory access, bad alignment) or an intentional syscall instruction (`svc`/`swi` on ARM, `int 0x80`/`sysenter` on x86, `syscall` on MIPS).

blocks.title: 5-Step Hardware Interrupt (IRQ) Handling Flow
blocks.caption: How an asynchronous device IRQ safely transitions the CPU to Kernel Mode, runs the ISR via the interrupt vector, and resumes the user task.

blocks.title: SMP Multicore & Monolithic vs. Microkernel Architectures (C2 & E2 Q2)
blocks.content:
### Symmetric Multi-Processing (SMP)
- Multiple CPU cores share the same **RAM** and can all execute kernel or user code.
- Each core has private **L1/L2/L3 caches** (requiring hardware **cache coherency**) and a **Local APIC** to balance IRQ handling across cores.

### Monolithic vs. Microkernel (E2 Q2)
| Dimension | Monolithic Kernel (Linux, Windows, SO3) | Microkernel (Minix, QNX, seL4) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **What lives in Kernel Space?** | All subsystems: Scheduler, MMU, VFS, Network, **Drivers**, IPC | **Minimal core only:** Scheduler, MMU, basic IPC, HAL |
| **Where do Drivers/FS/Net live?** | Kernel Space | **User Space** (as isolated server processes) communication via **Client-Server IPC** |
| **Performance** | **High** (direct function calls, few layers; great for hard real-time) | **Lower** (frequent user/kernel context switches & IPC messages) |
| **Security & Fault Isolation** | **Lower** (a buggy driver can crash the entire OS) | **High** (a crashed driver/FS process restarts without crashing the kernel) |
| **Extensibility** | Harder (kernel recompilation/modules) | **Easy** (add/restart user-space services) |

sections.title: 3. System Calls, Binary Images & Process Anatomy (C3 & E2)
sections.description: How syscalls cross the user/kernel boundary via ABI stubs, why buffered libc functions beat raw syscalls, ELF binary compilation, address types, and process memory layout.

blocks.title: System Calls, Stubs & the ABI (C3 & E2 Q6–Q7)
blocks.content:
A **system call (syscall)** is the controlled gateway for user programs to request kernel services (files, memory, processes, IPC).

### Exact Syscall Execution Sequence (E2 Q6)
1. Application calls a C wrapper (**stub**) in `libc` (e.g., `write(fd, buf, 10)`).
2. **Stub entry code** places the **syscall number** and **arguments** into specific CPU registers/stack according to the **ABI (Application Binary Interface)**.
   - *ARM SO3 ABI:* `R7` = syscall number, `R0, R1, R2` = arguments, `R0` = return value.
3. Stub executes the **software interrupt instruction** (`svc` on ARM, `int 0x80`/`sysenter` on x86, `syscall` on MIPS).
4. CPU switches to **Kernel Mode** and runs the kernel's syscall handler for that number.
5. Kernel writes the return value to `R0` (or stack) and returns to **User Mode**; stub exit code returns to caller (setting `errno` on error).

### Syscalls vs. High-Level Library Functions (E2 Q7)
- Standard APIs: **POSIX** (Unix/Linux), Win32 (Windows). Linux uses `libc` (`glibc`, `uClibc` embedded, `bionic` Android).
- **Why prefer `fopen()`/`fwrite()` (Section 3) over `open()`/`write()` (Section 2)?** Crossing the user/kernel boundary is **expensive** (mode switch + register/state handling). `stdio` functions use **user-space buffers** to batch many small writes into a single `write()` syscall!
- **`man` sections:** `man 1` (user commands), `man 2` (**syscalls**, e.g. `man 2 open`), `man 3` (**library functions**, e.g. `man 3 fopen`).

blocks.title: User-to-Kernel Syscall Flow (ARM SO3 ABI)
blocks.caption: The libc stub marshals arguments into R0–R2 and the syscall number into R7 before triggering svc.
blocks.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant App as User App
  participant Stub as libc Stub (User)
  participant Kern as Kernel Handler (SVC)
  App->>Stub: write(fd, buf, 10)
  Note over Stub: R7=no, R0=fd, R1=buf, R2=10
  Stub->>Kern: svc (Software Interrupt -> Kernel Mode)
  Kern->>Kern: Execute sys_write()
  Kern-->>Stub: Return bytes written in R0 (User Mode)
  Stub-->>App: return R0

blocks.title: Building an Executable Binary & Address Types (C3)
blocks.content:
### Compilation & Linking Pipeline
1. **Compiler:** Translates `.c` + `.h` into intermediate **object files** (`.o`), containing machine instructions and unresolved jumps (e.g., `bl printf`).
2. **Linker:** Resolves missing symbols against static/shared libraries (`libc.a`, `libmath.a`), inserts **C runtime (`crt`)** startup code (which calls `main()` and later `exit()`), and emits the final **executable binary image**:
   - **ELF** (Linux/Unix), **PE / COFF** (Windows), **Mach-O** (macOS).

### Three Address Types in Binaries
- **Relative address:** Offset from a base or current PC (e.g., `[fp, #-16]`).
- **Absolute address:** Fixed final memory location (unchanged at load time).
- **Symbolic address:** Named reference (e.g., `printf`) emitted by the compiler and resolved by the **linker**.

blocks.title: Process Definition & Memory Topography (C3 & E2 Q8, Q10)
blocks.content:
A **process** is a running instance of a program, composed of:
1. **Binary image** (executable on disk)
2. **Memory context** (private virtual address space)
3. **Execution context** (1 or more threads: PC, SP, registers)
4. **Logical resources** (open file descriptors, IPCs)

*(E2 Q10: An **application** is a user-level software product that may consist of **one or multiple processes**, each containing **one or multiple threads**.)*

### Standard Process Memory Sections (E2 Q8)
From lowest to highest virtual address:
- **`.text` (Code):** Machine instructions (read-only/executable).
- **`.data`:** Initialized global/static variables and constants.
- **`.bss` (Block Started by Symbol):** Uninitialized global/static variables. **Not stored as zeros on disk**—only its size is recorded in ELF, saving disk space until loaded into RAM!
- **Heap:** Dynamic allocations (`malloc`, `new`). Grows **upward** (toward higher addresses); shared by all threads.
- **Stack:** Local variables, function arguments, return addresses. Placed at top of address space and grows **downward**; **one stack per thread**.

blocks.title: Process Virtual Address Space Layout
blocks.caption: Heap grows upward from BSS while Stack grows downward from the top of the user address space.

sections.title: 4. PCB, Process Syscalls (fork, exec, waitpid, exit) & Context Switch (C4)
sections.description: The Process Control Block (PCB), process creation/termination lifecycle, orphan and zombie processes, and what makes context switches expensive.

blocks.title: Process Control Block (PCB) (C4 & E2 Q9)
blocks.content:
The **PCB (Process Control Block)** is the kernel-only data structure (invisible to user space) acting as a process's **ID card**. Every process has a unique PCB allocated at `fork()` and freed only when its parent calls `waitpid()`.

### Contents of a PCB
- **PID** (Process ID) & **Process State** (`New`, `Ready`, `Running`, `Waiting`, `Zombie`)
- **Execution Context:** Program Counter (`PC`), CPU registers, Stack Pointer (`SP`), priority
- **Memory Context:** Address space / MMU page tables, heap pointer
- **Resources:** Open file descriptor table (`fd_array`), references to child processes, **exit status code**.

blocks.title: The Unix Process Lifecycle: fork(), execve(), waitpid(), exit()

annotations.note: fork() returns 0 in child, child's PID (>0) in parent, or -1 on error.
exec*() replaces .text/.data/.bss/stack/heap with new program, keeping PID and open FDs.
Without waitpid(), a terminated child remains a ZOMBIE holding its PCB in kernel memory!

blocks.title: Zombie vs. Orphan Processes (C3 & C4)
blocks.content:
- **Zombie Process:** A child that has called `exit()`, so it is no longer schedulable, **but its parent has not yet called `waitpid()`**. Its PCB must remain in the kernel to hold the exit code.
- **Orphan Process:** A child whose **parent terminated before it**. The kernel reparents the orphan to the root process (`init`/`idle`), which will later call `waitpid()` to clean up its PCB.

blocks.title: Context Switch Mechanics & Cost (C4)
blocks.content:
A **context switch** occurs when the kernel suspends `P0` and resumes `P1`. It is triggered by:
1. Process termination (`exit()`)
2. Blocking on I/O or a resource (`Running` $\rightarrow$ `Waiting`)
3. Scheduler preemption (e.g., timer IRQ / quantum expired)

### Why Is a Process Context Switch Expensive (~1 ms)?
1. Save outgoing CPU registers, `PC`, `SP`, and **coprocessors/VFP (floating-point)** into `PCB0`.
2. Restore incoming registers and state from `PCB1`.
3. **Synchronize/flush CPU caches (L1/L2/L3)** with RAM.
4. **Reconfigure the MMU** to point to `P1`'s virtual address space.
5. Load `P1`'s `PC` and resume execution.

blocks.title: Context Switch Sequence (P0 → Kernel → P1)
blocks.caption: Saving PCB0, restoring PCB1, reconfiguring the MMU, and loading the new PC.
blocks.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant P0 as Process P0
  participant OS as OS Kernel
  participant P1 as Process P1
  Note over P0: Running
  P0->>OS: Syscall or Timer IRQ
  OS->>OS: Save P0 state into PCB0
  OS->>OS: Restore P1 state from PCB1
  OS->>OS: Reconfigure MMU & sync caches
  OS->>P1: Load new PC -> Resume P1
  Note over P1: Running

blocks.title: Analyze a fork() Execution Tree
blocks.prompt: Suppose `main()` calls `fork()` twice in a row with no `if` conditions: `fork(); fork(); printf("Hi\n");`. How many total processes exist, how many times is `Hi` printed, and what happens if the parent exits without `waitpid()`?
self_check_criteria: Calculated 2^2 = 4 total processes (1 original parent + 3 descendants).
Stated that 'Hi' is printed 4 times (once per process).
Explained that without waitpid(), children become zombies (if they finish first) or orphans reparented to init (if parent finishes first).
blocks.model_answer: Each fork() doubles the number of processes: after 2 consecutive fork() calls, there are 2^2 = 4 processes, so 'Hi' is printed 4 times. If the parent exits before its children, the children become orphans and are adopted by init/root. If children exit before the parent without waitpid(), they remain in the Zombie state until the parent collects their exit status or terminates.

sections.title: 5. Process States, Threads & POSIX pthreads (C5)
sections.description: The 5-state process lifecycle, TCB vs PCB, why threads are 10x faster than processes, POSIX pthread_create/join/exit, and shared-memory race conditions.

blocks.title: The 5 Process States & Legal Transitions (C5)
blocks.content:
The kernel maintains a queue per state (except `Running`, which holds at most 1 process per CPU core):

- **`New`:** PCB allocated, structures still initializing (not yet schedulable).
- **`Ready`:** Initialized and waiting in the ready queue for CPU time.
- **`Running`:** Currently executing instructions on a CPU core.
- **`Waiting`:** Blocked on I/O, a pipe, a mutex, etc. *(A **watchdog timer** can detect processes stuck here too long, e.g., deadlocks.)*
- **`Zombie`:** Terminated via `exit()`, awaiting parent's `waitpid()`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Crucial Rule:** A process waking up from `Waiting` **NEVER** jumps directly to `Running`! It **must** transition `Waiting -> Ready` so the scheduler retains full control over CPU allocation.

blocks.title: 5-State Process Transition Diagram
blocks.caption: Notice that Waiting transitions exclusively to Ready, never directly to Running.
blocks.source:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> New
  New --> Ready: Initialized
  Ready --> Running: Dispatched by Scheduler
  Running --> Ready: Preempted (Timer / Higher Priority)
  Running --> Waiting: I/O Request / Blocking Syscall
  Waiting --> Ready: Resource Available / I/O Done
  Running --> Zombie: exit()
  Zombie --> [*]: Parent calls waitpid()

blocks.title: Threads, TCB & Hyper-Threading (C5)
blocks.content:
Creating a process takes **~250 $\mu$s**; creating a **thread** (lightweight execution context inside a process) takes **~25 $\mu$s** (10x faster).

### What Threads Share vs. What Each Thread Owns
| Shared by All Threads in a Process | Private to Each Thread (in its **TCB**) |
| :--- | :--- |
| Virtual Address Space (`.text`, `.data`, `.bss`, **Heap**) | **Stack** (local vars, call frames) |
| Open File Descriptors (`fd_array`), IPCs | **PC** (Program Counter) & **CPU Registers** |
| Process ID (PID) & Exit Code | Thread ID, **State**, **Priority**, Stack Pointer (`SP`) |

- **TCB (Thread Control Block):** Much smaller than a PCB because it holds no memory-space or open-file tables.
- **Hyper-Threading:** Hardware support where 1 physical CPU core exposes 2 logical CPUs (`CPU #0`, `CPU #1`) for fast hardware thread switching.

count++ compiles to multiple machine instructions (load, add, store). Preemption mid-update causes lost increments (race condition).
Do NOT replace pthread_join() with pthread_exit() here if main() still needs to run printf() afterward!

sections.title: 6. File Descriptors, Redirection (dup2) & Pipes (C6 & E4)
sections.description: Per-process fd_array vs. kernel global open file table (VFS), dup2() stream redirection, anonymous vs. named pipes, and the E4 pipe+dup2 coding exercise.

blocks.title: File Descriptors, VFS Open File Table & dup2() (C6)
blocks.content:
A **file descriptor (FD)** is a small integer identifying an open resource (file, pipe, socket) via two kernel tables managed by the **VFS (Virtual File System)**:
1. **Per-process `fd_array[]`** (inside the PCB): Maps local FD numbers (`0=stdin`, `1=stdout`, `2=stderr`, `3, 4...`) to entries in the global table.
2. **Global Open File Table (`open_fds`)**: Stores resource attributes, access mode (`RO`, `WO`, `RW`), and current file offset (`pos`).

### Stream Redirection with `dup2(oldfd, newfd)`
`dup2(oldfd, newfd)` makes `newfd` point to the **same global open file table entry** as `oldfd` (closing `newfd` first if open).
- Example: `dup2(file_fd, STDOUT_FILENO);` redirects all `printf()` output into the file.
- **Crucial Property:** `fd_array` redirections are **inherited across `fork()`** and **preserved across `exec()`**! That is how shells implement `ls > out.txt` and `ls | more`.

blocks.title: How dup2(3, 1) Redirects stdout to readme.txt
blocks.caption: Local fd[1] (stdout) is updated to point to the same global open_fds entry as fd[3].
blocks.source:
flowchart LR
  subgraph Local ["Process P0 fd_array"]
    fd0["0: stdin"]
    fd1["1: stdout (redirected)"]
    fd2["2: stderr"]
    fd3["3: opened file"]
  end
  subgraph Global ["Kernel Global open_fds"]
    g0["Console RO"]
    g1["Console WO"]
    g2["readme.txt RW / pos"]
  end
  fd0 --> g0
  fd2 --> g1
  fd3 --> g2
  fd1 -. "dup2(3, 1)" .-> g2

  classDef redir fill:#d1fae5,stroke:#059669,stroke-width:2px;
  class fd1,g2 redir;

blocks.title: IPC Overview & Anonymous vs. Named Pipes (C6)
blocks.content:
Because processes have isolated address spaces, they need kernel **IPC (Inter-Process Communication)**:
- **Data exchange:** Memory-mapped files, shared memory.
- **Synchronization:** Locks (mutex), semaphores, monitors, signals.
- **Both exchange & sync:** **Pipes**, **Network Sockets**, message queues.

### Pipe Properties
- **Unidirectional FIFO** byte stream with **destructive reads** (reading removes data).
- **Bounded buffer (~4 KiB):** Reading an empty pipe blocks (`Waiting`); writing a full pipe blocks (`Waiting`).
- `pipe(int fd[2])`: **`fd[0]` = read end** (like `stdin=0`), **`fd[1]` = write end** (like `stdout=1`).

| Feature | Anonymous Pipe (`pipe()`) | Named Pipe / FIFO (`mkfifo()`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Who can use it?** | Related processes (parent/child after `fork()`) | **Any** processes knowing its filesystem path |
| **Persistence** | Destroyed automatically when all FDs close | **Persistent** in filesystem until `unlink()` |
| **Connection** | Inherited via `fork()` | `open()` blocks by default until peer opens other end |

blocks.title: E4 Exercise: Redirect Child stdout to Parent via Pipe & dup2()

annotations.note: Create the pipe BEFORE fork() so both processes share the same kernel pipe.
Remember: STDOUT_FILENO is 1. Close fd[1] after dup2(fd[1], STDOUT_FILENO).
Parent MUST close fd[1] so read(fd[0], ...) can observe EOF when the child exits.

blocks.title: Check Your E4 Solution (Pipe + dup2)
blocks.prompt: Write the C code to complete `e4_pipe_dup2_starter.c` above so that anything written to `stdout` in the child is captured and printed by the parent. Draft your solution before revealing the self-check criteria and model answer.
self_check_criteria: In child (pid == 0): closed fd[0], called dup2(fd[1], STDOUT_FILENO), closed fd[1], wrote to stdout (e.g. printf + fflush).
In parent (pid > 0): closed fd[1] (crucial for EOF!), looped read(fd[0], ...) until 0, closed fd[0], and called waitpid(pid, NULL, 0).
blocks.model_answer: pipe(fd); pid = fork(); if (pid == 0) { close(fd[0]); dup2(fd[1], STDOUT_FILENO); close(fd[1]); printf("Hello from child!\n"); fflush(stdout); exit(0); } else { close(fd[1]); while ((n = read(fd[0], buf, sizeof(buf)-1)) > 0) { buf[n] = '\0'; printf("Parent: %s", buf); } close(fd[0]); waitpid(pid, NULL, 0); }

sections.title: 7. Signals & TCP/IP Network Sockets (C7)
sections.description: Asynchronous signal delivery, masking vs ignoring, uncatchable signals, essential POSIX signal table, sockaddr_in, byte-order helpers, and TCP client-server syscalls.

blocks.title: POSIX Signals: Asynchronous Process Events (C7)
blocks.content:
A **signal** is an asynchronous event delivered to a process by the kernel or another process (`kill(pid, sig)`). When the target process is **`Running`**, the kernel diverts execution to a user-space **signal handler** (callback, analogous to a kernel ISR).

### Three Rules of Signal Delivery
1. **No Queuing of Duplicates:** At most **one** pending instance of a given signal type is stored in the process's pending set.
2. **Masking vs. Ignoring:**
   - **Masked:** Signal stays pending and is delivered as soon as it is unmasked.
   - **Ignored (`SIG_IGN`):** Signal is discarded immediately.
   - **Default (`SIG_DFL`):** Restores default OS action.
3. **Uncatchable/Unignorable Signals:** **`SIGKILL`** (`kill -9`) and **`SIGSTOP`** can **never** be caught, masked, or ignored.

### Essential Signals for TE1
| Signal | Trigger / Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| `SIGINT` / `SIGQUIT` | Terminal `Ctrl+C` / `Ctrl+D` |
| `SIGTSTP` / `SIGCONT` | Terminal suspend `Ctrl+Z` / Resume stopped process |
| `SIGKILL` / `SIGTERM` | Abrupt kill (`-9`, uncatchable) / Graceful termination request |
| `SIGSEGV` / `SIGFPE` / `SIGILL` | Invalid memory access (segfault) / Divide by zero / Illegal instruction |
| `SIGPIPE` | Writing to a pipe or socket with **no open reader** |
| `SIGCHLD` | Sent to parent when a **child terminates** (triggers `waitpid()`) |
| `SIGALRM` / `SIGUSR1`, `SIGUSR2` | `alarm()` timer expired / User-defined signals |

blocks.title: TCP/IP BSD Sockets & Data Structures (C7)
blocks.content:
A **socket** is a bidirectional communication endpoint identified by a **socket descriptor** (used with `read()`/`write()`/`close()` or `send()`/`recv()`). Local same-machine communication uses `localhost` (`127.0.0.1`, loopback).

### Addressing (`<sys/socket.h>`, `struct sockaddr_in`)
- `sin_family`: `AF_INET` (IPv4)
- `sin_port`: 16-bit port in **network byte order (big-endian)** $\rightarrow$ convert with **`htons()`** / **`ntohs()`**
- `sin_addr`: 32-bit IPv4 address $\rightarrow$ convert string `"127.0.0.1"` with **`inet_pton()`** / **`inet_ntop()`**

### Critical `read()`/`recv()` vs. `write()`/`send()` Trap
- In `write(fd, buf, count)`, `count` is the **exact** number of bytes to send.
- In `read(fd, buf, maxlen)`, `maxlen` is the **maximum** buffer capacity—`read()` may return **fewer** bytes! On TCP, **`read()`/`recv()` returning `0` means the peer closed the connection** (EOF).

blocks.title: Concurrent TCP Client–Server Syscall Sequence
blocks.caption: Server binds and listens on a passive socket; accept() returns a new active socket FD (newfd) per client, typically handled in a forked child or thread.
blocks.source:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant S as Server (Master)
  participant W as Slave (fork/thread)
  S->>S: fd = socket()
  S->>S: bind(fd, addr)
  S->>S: listen(fd, backlog)
  C->>C: cfd = socket()
  C->>S: connect(cfd, addr)
  S->>S: newfd = accept(fd) [blocks]
  S->>W: fork() / pthread_create()
  Note over S: Master closes newfd & loops to accept()
  Note over W: Slave closes passive fd
  C->>W: send(cfd, data)
  W->>C: recv(newfd) / send(newfd)
  C->>W: close(cfd) -> recv returns 0
  W->>W: close(newfd) & exit()

sections.title: 8. CPU Scheduling & Algorithms (C8 & E5)
sections.description: Waiting time metric, preemption points, FCFS, SJF/SRTF & exponential averaging, Round Robin quantum trade-offs, Priority scheduling & aging, and Multi-Level Feedback Queues.

blocks.title: Scheduling Metrics & Preemption Points (C8)
blocks.content:
Processes alternate between **CPU bursts** and **I/O bursts**. Because the scheduler only selects from the **`Ready`** queue, the primary performance metric is:

$$\text{Waiting Time} = \text{Total time spent in the } \texttt{Ready} \text{ state} \quad (\text{I/O time excluded})$$

For a single CPU burst arriving at $t_{\text{arr}}$ and finishing at $t_{\text{finish}}$ with burst duration $B$:
$$W = (t_{\text{finish}} - t_{\text{arr}}) - B$$

### Preemption Points
The scheduler (`schedule()`) runs at the end of an ISR (e.g., timer IRQ) or syscall:
- **Mandatory (non-preemptive) switch:** `Running -> Waiting` (I/O) or `Running -> Zombie` (`exit()`).
- **Preemptive switch:** `Running -> Ready` (quantum expired or higher-priority process arrived).

blocks.title: Core Scheduling Policies Compared (C8)
blocks.content:
### 1. FCFS (First-Come, First-Served)
- **Non-preemptive FIFO.** Simple, but suffers from the **convoy effect** (short jobs wait behind a long CPU-bound job).

### 2. SJF (Shortest Job First) & SRTF (Preemptive SJF)
- **Optimal** for minimizing average waiting time.
- **Non-preemptive SJF:** Picks shortest burst among `Ready` processes when CPU is free.
- **Preemptive SJF (SRTF):** Compares **remaining** burst time whenever a new process arrives; preempts if the newcomer's burst is strictly shorter.
- **Limitation 1:** Future burst lengths are unknown $\rightarrow$ estimated via **Exponential Moving Average**:

$$\tau_{n+1} = \alpha\, t_n + (1 - \alpha)\, \tau_n, \quad 0 < \alpha < 1$$

  where $t_n$ is the last measured burst and $\tau_n$ is the previous estimate. ($lpha$ near 1 reacts fast to recent changes; $\alpha$ near 0 smooths over history.)
- **Limitation 2:** **Starvation** of long processes if short jobs keep arriving.

### 3. Round Robin (RR)
- **Preemptive FIFO** with a fixed **time quantum $q$** (typically $10\text{–}200\text{ ms}$; rule of thumb: **80%** of CPU bursts finish within $q$).
- $q$ too small $\rightarrow$ excessive context-switch overhead; $q$ too large $\rightarrow$ degenerates to FCFS.

### 4. Priority & Multi-Level Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
- **Priority:** Always picks highest priority (**in SYE: higher number = higher priority**; FIFO tie-breaker). Static priority risks **starvation** $\rightarrow$ solved by **aging**.
- **MLFQ (E5 Q3):** Multiple priority queues with different policies (e.g., high = RR $q=8$, medium = RR $q=16$, low = FCFS) and **dynamic priority** (processes waiting too long are promoted to prevent starvation).

blocks.description: Explore how smoothing factor alpha (0 < alpha < 1) weights the latest measured burst t_n = 4 against previous estimate tau_n = 10 (from C8 slide 8).

blocks.prompt: Trace Round Robin with quantum q = 2 on: P1(arr=0, dur=6), P2(arr=1, dur=9), P3(arr=3, dur=2), P4(arr=8, dur=4). What is each process's waiting time and the average waiting time? (Note: if a process arrives at the exact moment another's quantum expires, standard convention places the newly arrived process in the ready queue before re-enqueuing the preempted process.)

Waiting times: P1 = 12-0-6 = 6, P2 = 21-1-9 = 11, P3 = 8-3-2 = 3, P4 = 18-8-4 = 6. Average = (6+11+3+6)/4 = 6.50.

sections.title: 9. TE1 Active Recall Flashcards & Diagnostic Exam
sections.description: High-frequency FSRS flashcards and Bloom-calibrated diagnostic questions covering every TE1 chapter and exercise.

blocks.title: User Mode → Kernel Mode Transitions
blocks.front: What are the **only** two ways a CPU can transition from **User Mode** to **Kernel Mode**?
blocks.back:
1. **Hardware Interrupt (IRQ)** — asynchronous (e.g., timer tick, disk I/O).
2. **Software Interrupt / Exception / Trap** — synchronous (e.g., syscall `svc`/`int 0x80`, divide-by-zero, page/seg fault).

A user program can **never** directly modify the CPU status register.

blocks.title: fork() Return Values & Zombie/Orphan
blocks.front: What are the three return values of `fork()`, and what is the difference between a **Zombie** and an **Orphan**?
blocks.back:
- **`fork()` returns:** `0` in child, `> 0` (child PID) in parent, `< 0` on error (`errno`).
- **Zombie:** Child exited, but parent hasn't called `waitpid()` yet (PCB still held).
- **Orphan:** Parent exited first; kernel reparents child to `init`/`idle`.

blocks.title: Pipe Ends & dup2() Semantics
blocks.front: Which `pipe(fd)` index is read vs. write, and what does `dup2(oldfd, newfd)` do?
blocks.back:
- **`fd[0]`** = read end (like `stdin=0`); **`fd[1]`** = write end (like `stdout=1`).
- **`dup2(oldfd, newfd)`** makes `newfd` a synonym for `oldfd` in `fd_array[]` (pointing to the same global `open_fds` entry). Preserved across `fork()` and `exec()`.

blocks.title: Signal Rules & Uncatchable Signals
blocks.front: Which two signals cannot be caught, masked, or ignored, and what triggers `SIGPIPE` and `SIGCHLD`?
blocks.back:
- **Uncatchable:** `SIGKILL` (`kill -9`) and `SIGSTOP`.
- **`SIGPIPE`:** Writing to a pipe/socket with no open reader.
- **`SIGCHLD`:** Sent to parent when a child process terminates.
blocks.hint: One terminates immediately; one pauses execution.

blocks.title: E1: Memory Region Size Calculation
blocks.question: A RAM region spans inclusive byte addresses from `0x1000` to `0xf'ffff`. How many bytes does this region contain?
blocks.explanation:
For an inclusive range [start, end], size = end - start + 1 = 0xFFFFF - 0x1000 + 1 = 0x100000 - 0x1000 = 0xFF000 = 1020 * 1024 = 1,044,480 bytes (1020 KiB).

* '1,044,479 bytes' forgets the +1 for inclusive endpoints.
* '1,048,576 bytes' ignores the 0x1000 (4 KiB) offset.
* '65,536 bytes' is 0x10000.
hints: Use the inclusive range formula: Size = End - Start + 1.
Notice that 0xFFFFF + 1 = 0x100000 (1 MiB = 1024 KiB), and 0x1000 = 4 KiB.

blocks.title: C2: User-to-Kernel Mode Transition
blocks.question: How can a CPU executing in **User Mode** transition to **Kernel Mode**?
options: Only via a hardware interrupt (IRQ) or a software interrupt / exception (trap)
By directly executing a privileged instruction to clear the user-mode bit in the status register
By calling any C library function such as printf() or malloc()
By jumping to a kernel virtual address using a function pointer
blocks.correct_answer: Only via a hardware interrupt (IRQ) or a software interrupt / exception (trap)
blocks.explanation:
The CPU only enters Kernel Mode through hardware interrupts (IRQ) or synchronous software interrupts/exceptions (such as `svc`/`int 0x80` or a memory fault).

* Modifying the status register is a privileged instruction forbidden in User Mode.
* Calling `malloc()` or `printf()` stays in User Mode unless it internally invokes a syscall stub.
* Jumping to a kernel address from User Mode triggers an MMU protection fault (a trap!), not valid execution.
hints: Can user code modify the CPU status register directly?
Think about the two categories of interrupts discussed in C2.

blocks.title: C3 & C5: Process Memory Sections & Threads
blocks.question: Which statements about a multi-threaded process's virtual address space are TRUE? (Select all that apply)
options: Each thread has its own private Stack.
All threads share the same Heap, .data, .bss, and .text sections.
The .bss section stores uninitialized global/static variables without reserving their full zero-filled size on disk.
Each thread has its own independent open file descriptor table (fd_array).
correct_answer: Each thread has its own private Stack.
All threads share the same Heap, .data, .bss, and .text sections.
The .bss section stores uninitialized global/static variables without reserving their full zero-filled size on disk.
blocks.explanation: Threads within the same process share the virtual address space (.text, .data, .bss, Heap) and process-level logical resources like `fd_array[]`. Only execution-context state (Stack, PC, registers, SP, priority) is private per thread in its TCB.
hints: Separate what belongs to the process (PCB) vs. each execution context (TCB).
Remember why C3 explained that a 1,000-int uninitialized array doesn't bloat the ELF file on disk.

blocks.title: C5: Legal State Transitions
blocks.question: When a process in the `Waiting` state receives the I/O data it was waiting for, which state does it transition to?
blocks.explanation: A waking process ALWAYS transitions `Waiting -> Ready`, never directly to `Running`, so the scheduler remains in control of which process gets the CPU.
hints: Can a waking process bypass the scheduler?

blocks.title: C6 & E4: Pipe Blocking & EOF Bug
blocks.question: In E4, the parent reads from `fd[0]` in a `while (read(fd[0], ...) > 0)` loop after the child writes and exits. If the parent **forgets** to call `close(fd[1])`, what happens?
options: The parent blocks forever in `read()` because a write end (`fd[1]`) is still open in the parent.
The kernel automatically closes `fd[1]` when the child calls `exit()`.
blocks.correct_answer: The parent blocks forever in `read()` because a write end (`fd[1]`) is still open in the parent.
blocks.explanation: A pipe returns EOF (`read() == 0`) only when **all** write file descriptors referring to that pipe are closed. Even though the child exited and closed its `fd[1]`, the parent still holds its own `fd[1]` open, so `read()` blocks waiting for data that will never arrive.
hints: Remember that fork() duplicated both fd[0] and fd[1] into the parent and child.
When does read() on a pipe return 0 (EOF)?

blocks.title: C7: TCP Socket Peer Closure
blocks.question: On a connected TCP socket, when the remote peer closes the connection, a blocking `read()` or `recv()` call returns the integer value ___.
blocks.explanation: On a TCP stream socket, `read()`/`recv()` returning `0` signals End-Of-File (peer closed the connection). A positive return value is the number of bytes received (up to `maxlen`), and `-1` indicates an error.
hints: It is the same return value as EOF on a regular file or pipe.

blocks.title: C8: SJF Exponential Moving Average
blocks.question: Using SJF burst estimation $\tau_{n+1} = \alpha t_n + (1 - \alpha)\tau_n$ with $\alpha = 0.5$, previous estimate $\tau_n = 10$, and measured burst $t_n = 4$, what is $\tau_{n+1}$?
hints: Substitute alpha=0.5, t_n=4, tau_n=10 into the formula.

blocks.title: C4: Predict fork() + Separate Address Spaces
blocks.explanation: `fork()` gives the child its own copy of the address space, so `x += 5` only modifies the child's `x` (15), leaving the parent's `x` at 10. Because the parent calls `waitpid()`, `C:15 ` is printed before `P:10`.
hints: Do parent and child share variables after fork()?
Which process prints first given waitpid()?
